concerns.text: The plan pivots to a 'Synthetic Microstructure Generator' to bypass the lack of real data. This fundamentally alters the research question from 'Can microstructure images predict fracture toughness in real alloys?' to 'Can a CNN learn a Hall-Petch approximation on synthetic noise?' The synthetic data lacks the complex, non-linear microstructural defects (voids, inclusions, complex grain boundaries) that actually drive fracture toughness variance. A model trained on synthetic data cannot validate the predictive power of *real* imaging data, rendering the core scientific claim unanswerable by this method.

The plan proposes using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the distribution of MAE differences across 5 runs. However, the 'runs' are independent training seeds on the *same* synthetic dataset. This tests the stability of the optimizer, not the statistical significance of the model's predictive power against a null hypothesis of 'no signal'. Without a held-out real-world test set or a permutation test against shuffled labels on real data, the p-value will be meaningless for the intended scientific conclusion.

The plan assumes a deterministic function (Hall-Petch) to generate K_IC values for synthetic images. This creates a circular validation loop: the model is trained to predict a value derived from the very features (grain size) it is supposed to discover. If the CNN learns the Hall-Petch relation, it is merely fitting the generator's logic, not discovering new microstructural predictors. This fails the 'Construct Validity' check for measuring 'predictive signal from imaging data'.

Constitution Principle I (Reproducibility) requires results to be reproducible by re-running against the project's data. If the data is synthetic and generated on-the-fly, the 'ground truth' is the generator's code. This violates the principle of validating against *observed* physical phenomena. The plan conflates 'reproducible code' with 'reproducible scientific finding'.

The plan frames results as 'methodological validation' rather than material science claims. However, the User Story 2 and Success Criteria (SC-001, SC-002) explicitly claim to determine 'if imaging data alone explains variance in toughness'. If the data is synthetic, the claim 'imaging data explains variance' is tautological (the variance was programmed in). The research question itself is broken under the proposed synthetic data approach.
